# The Phantom Test Failure

You're a developer on a team that maintains an e-commerce platform. Every morning, you run the automated test suite before starting work. Today, like every day this week, all 847 tests pass on your local machine with green checkmarks across the board.

You push your latest commit—a minor CSS adjustment to a button's padding—to the shared repository. Within minutes, the continuous integration server reports that 12 tests in the payment processing module have failed. These tests have nothing to do with your CSS change, and you haven't touched any payment-related code in months.

You pull down the exact same commit, run the tests locally again, and they all pass. Your colleague on the other side of the office pulls the same branch and runs the tests—they pass for her too. Yet the CI server continues to fail those same 12 tests with each subsequent run.

The test output shows only that expected values don't match actual values, with no obvious errors or stack traces pointing to a root cause. The CI server logs show no infrastructure warnings or resource issues.

origin1: The CI server has a different version of a payment gateway sandbox/mock service or a cached dependency that behaves differently than the local development environments, causing the payment processing tests to return subtly different response values that only manifest in that specific environment.

origin2: The CI server's system clock is drifting or set to a different timezone than the local machines, causing time-sensitive payment processing logic (such as token expiration checks, transaction timestamp validations, or date-based pricing calculations) to produce different computed values.
